title: 330. Driving Transformational Change with the Flywheel Effect
author: Business Leader Daily
summary: This short leadership post applies Jim Collins's flywheel concept to organizational change. The author argues that leaders must first understand how their company's systems and incentives work, because changing process steps without aligning incentives will not last. The flywheel framework asks leaders to see how functions such as product, operations, marketing and sales reinforce each other, illustrated with Vanguard's low-cost cycle. Collins's own passages supply the contrast between steady momentum-building and the doom loop of launching fanfare-driven programs and changing direction. The move is to treat transformation as many aligned efforts compounding over time rather than one grand initiative, with the warning that ignoring the whole system can set an organization back.
points: Changing processes without aligning the incentives behind them will not produce long-term change.
The flywheel treats transformation as repeated pushes by interdependent functions that build momentum, not a single defining action.
The Vanguard example shows each step, from low costs to economies of scale, depending on the others, so one failing area weakens the whole plan.
Collins's doom loop describes organizations that keep launching new programs and changing direction, never building sustained momentum.
Leaders should look at the entire system, since isolated changes can move the organization further from its goals.
quotes: Just changing process steps without making sure incentives are aligned will not have the long-term impact you are looking for.
Introduced by Jim Collins in his book Good to Great, the idea centers around looking at how processes can be supportive to build continuous momentum.

No matter how dramatic the end result, good-to-great transformations never happen in one fell swoop. In building a great company or social sector enterprise, there is no single defining action, no grand program, no one killer innovation, no solitary lucky break, no miracle moment. Rather, the process resembles relentlessly pushing a giant, heavy flywheel, turn upon turn, building momentum until a point of breakthrough, and beyond.
You can see how each step is dependent on the other. If one area fails to deliver, it reduces the impact of the entire plan.
For companies that can generate a Flywheel Effect, the alignment work can require hard changes, but the reward can be a sustainable advantage difficult for competitors to follow.
When you don’t look at the entire system, you may not make the necessary changes to succeed. Even worse, your changes can cause setbacks that take you farther away from your goals.
